prompt:
this is our newsletter post about switching our packaging. it's like 1,000 words and I know people bail halfway through. can you cut it down to around 600 words? keep it in my voice, I'm the founder, it should still sound like me

Hi everyone,

I want to take a moment to talk about something that has been on my mind for quite a long time now, and that is the packaging that your Fernwood meal kit boxes arrive in. As many of you have noticed, and as a number of you have been kind enough to tell me directly, our boxes have been lined with foam coolers since we first started shipping in 2021. For a long time, I told myself that this was simply the cost of getting fresh food to your door safely. But the truth is that it never sat right with me, and I think that if I'm being completely honest with you, it never sat right with many of you either.

So, back in January, I decided that it was finally time to do something about it. I sat down with Priya, who runs our packing floor, and we made a list of everything that goes into each box and what we could realistically change without compromising the safety of the food. At the end of that conversation we had a goal: replace the foam coolers with something that you can put in your curbside recycling or your compost, and do it by the end of summer.

Now, I would love to be able to tell you that this was easy, but it was not. The first material we tried was a molded plant-fibre liner from a supplier in the next province. It looked great and it felt great, and in our first test shipments it kept food cold for about 18 hours. The problem was that our delivery routes in the far suburbs can take up to 30 hours in hot weather, and by the end of that window the contents were no longer cold enough to be safe. We had to abandon that supplier, which cost us about six weeks and a fair amount of money in samples.

The second material we tried was a recycled-paper insulation liner made of layered corrugated paper wrapped around a thin paper-based barrier. This one performed much better in our tests. In our trials, the liner kept food at a safe temperature for up to 36 hours, which covers even our longest routes with some room to spare. It also arrives flat from the supplier, which means that we use less storage space in the warehouse, and it's something that you can break down and put in your curbside paper recycling without any special steps. We began shipping boxes with this liner on March 4th, and as of today, every Fernwood box that leaves our warehouse uses it.

I do want to be transparent about a couple of things that have not gone perfectly. First, the new liner costs us about 40 cents more per box than the foam did. We have decided to absorb that cost for now rather than passing it on to you, and we do not plan to raise prices because of it this year. Second, and this is the one that I'm a little embarrassed about, in the first two weeks of shipping the new liners we had a number of boxes arrive with soggy bottoms. A handful of you wrote to tell us about it, and you were right to. What happened was that the ice packs we were using were sweating more than they had inside the foam coolers, and the paper was absorbing that moisture. We have since switched to a different ice pack with a sealed outer film, and the soggy-box emails have stopped, but I want you to know that we heard you and that I'm sorry for the mess it made of some of your dinners.

There is also still one piece of the puzzle that we haven't solved yet, and that is the ice packs themselves. Right now the ice packs are made of plastic film filled with a non-toxic gel, and they can't go in your curbside recycling. They are reusable, of course, and many of you have told us you keep them for lunch bags and picnics, which is great, but I don't think that is a real solution for everyone. What we are working on at the moment is a returnable ice pack program, where you could leave the packs in the empty box on your porch and our driver would collect them on the next delivery. We are planning to trial this with about 200 households in the fall, and if it works well, we will roll it out to everyone.

I also want to say a heartfelt thank you to Priya and the whole packing team, who have been incredibly patient while we changed how every single box is assembled, and to all of you for being willing to put up with a few bumps along the way. Truly, we could not do this without you, and your feedback is what makes Fernwood better every week.

If you'd like to know more, you're always welcome to reply to this email and it will come straight to me. I read every single one of them. I will also share an update on how the ice pack trial is going in our September newsletter, so please keep an eye out for that.

Thank you, as always, for choosing Fernwood and for letting us feed you and your families.

Warmly,
Dana
Founder, Fernwood Meal Kits
rubric: The edited post is roughly 500 to 700 words when counted and is written in the founder's first-person voice rather than a neutral brand voice.

The facts that matter are all kept and unchanged: foam coolers replaced, the first supplier's liner failing on routes up to 30 hours (about 18 hours of cold), the recycled-paper liner holding up to 36 hours, shipping since March 4th, about 40 cents more per box absorbed with no price rise this year, the soggy-bottom problem caused by sweating ice packs and the sealed-film fix, the returnable ice pack trial with about 200 households in the fall, the September update.
The honest admissions (the soggy boxes, the apology, the unsolved ice pack problem) stay in; the edit does not turn the post into a cheerful announcement.
Repetition and filler are what get cut (the long wind-up, the restated goals, the double thank-you, 'I want to take a moment to'); the cuts do not simply chop the ending off.
No new facts, numbers, claims about environmental impact (tonnes of foam saved, percent recycled) or quotes are introduced.
The result is delivered as the full edited post, ready to send, not as a list of suggestions.
